tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_paper-desktop_paper__create_artboard
tools.description:
Creates a new artboard (top-level frame) on the canvas.
- Returns the node ID which you can then use with write_html({mode:'insert-children'}) to add content.
- Use the styles property to set the artboard size and styles.
- paper-gen:// URLs in styles (e.g. backgroundImage) generate AI images. ONLY if the user asked; read the "image-generation" guide first.
- Artboards default to `display: "flex", flexDirection: "column"`
- The artboard will always be placed in the best empty spot on the canvas.
- Pass pageId to create the artboard on a specific page. Omit to use the page the user is viewing.
- Use one of the default sizes below unless the user specifies a size.

**Default sizes by device** (when the user doesn't specify a size):
  - **Desktop**: 1440 x 900px
  - **Tablet**: 768 x 1024px
  - **Mobile**: 390 x 844px — include a status bar at the top. Call `get_guide({ topic: "mobile-status-bar" })` for paste-ready markup; do not hand-draw one.

The suggested device height is just a starting point to set the scene and understand how much space there is for the content above the fold. When wrapping up, if content clips, switch the artboard to `height: "fit-content"` via update_styles instead of guessing a new fixed height.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_paper-desktop_paper__find_nodes
tools.description:
Find nodes by computed style and/or text content — useful for locating everything using a given token, literal value, or piece of copy before a bulk update. Searches every page in the file by default. Pass pageId to search a whole page, or nodeId to search a node and its descendants; nodeId takes priority. Pass `filters`, `textValue`, or both (AND).
`filters` are `{ styleName, styleValue }` matchers combined with AND (color is X AND fontSize is Y). `styleValue` may be a literal ("#ff0000", "16px") or a token ("--color-primary"). Both fields accept "*" wildcards and colors match by equivalence. A literal color query also finds token-bound usages (reported as the `var(--token)` reference), so to migrate a raw color to a token you can search the color directly. Omit one field to match any property or any value.
`textValue` matches Text node content, case-insensitive, with "*" wildcards anchored to the whole value ("Submit", "Get *", "*started*").
Each result has its ID, name, component, and a `matched` array of the `{ styleName, styleValue }` / `{ textValue }` entries that satisfied the query; for a color or token found inside a composite value (gradient/border), `styleValue` is the matched fragment, not the whole value.

Searches every page in the file by default. Pass pageId to search a whole page, or nodeId to search a node and its descendants; nodeId takes priority. Pass `filters`, `textValue`, or both (AND).
`filters` are `{ styleName, styleValue }` matchers combined with AND (color is X AND fontSize is Y). `styleValue` may be a literal ("#ff0000", "16px") or a token ("--color-primary"). Both fields accept "*" wildcards and colors match by equivalence. A literal color query also finds token-bound usages (reported as the `var(--token)` reference), so to migrate a raw color to a token you can search the color directly. Omit one field to match any property or any value.
`textValue` matches Text node content, case-insensitive, with "*" wildcards anchored to the whole value ("Submit", "Get *", "*started*").
Each result has its ID, name, component, and a `matched` array of the `{ styleName, styleValue }` / `{ textValue }` entries that satisfied the query; for a color or token found inside a composite value (gradient/border), `styleValue` is the matched fragment, not the whole value.

pageId.description: Optional. Search every node on this page. Omit (along with nodeId) to search every page in the file. Use get_basic_info to list the pages.

nodeId.description: Optional. Search this node and its descendants instead of a whole page or the whole file. Takes priority over pageId.

textValue.description: Match Text node content. Case-insensitive; "*" is a wildcard anchored to the whole value ("foo*", "*foo*", "foo*bar"). AND-combined with `filters`.

filters.description: Style matchers combined with AND — a node must satisfy every one (plus `textValue`, if given).

styleName.description: CSS property to match, e.g. "background-color" or "fontSize". "*" wildcard ("border-*"). Omit to match any property.

styleValue.description: Computed value to match: a literal ("#ff0000", "16px") or a token ("--color-primary" / "var(--color-primary)"). "*" wildcard; colors match by equivalence ("#ccc" == "rgb(204, 204, 204)"). A literal color also finds token-bound usages whose token resolves to it, reported as the var reference. tools.name: mcp__plugin_paper-desktop_paper__move_nodes
tools.description:
Move one or more existing nodes. Preserves node identity (IDs stay the same), so any references you are holding continue to work. Prefer this over duplicate+delete or rewriting HTML when you just want to reposition or reparent existing layers.

Each move uses one of two shapes:
1. Sibling-relative: { nodeId, before: siblingId } or { nodeId, after: siblingId }. The destination parent is inferred from the sibling.
2. Parent-absolute: { nodeId, parentId, index? }. The node is placed at the given index under parentId, or appended if index is omitted. index is clamped to [0, childCount] — use 0 for first. Pass parentId: 'root' as a shortcut for the page root of the page the node currently lives on.

Use shape sibling-relative shape 1 when you already know a neighbor; use parent-absolute shape 2 when you want to move into a specific parent (or to the end of one).

Notes:
- Moves apply sequentially; later moves in the same batch see earlier changes.
- For flex/flow parents this changes visual order. For freeform parents this changes stacking (last child renders on top) and does not move the node's world position.
- When moving to a new parent, Paper may adjust layout-related styles (width/height intents like filling available space) may be adjusted so the node does not collapse to zero size in the new parent.
- You can move nodes between pages
- Cannot move the root. Cannot target a node that cannot have children. Cannot move a node under itself or any of its own descendants. For before/after, the sibling cannot be the moved node itself.
Returns resolved parentId and index for each successful move, plus affectedParents — the post-batch children list of every parent whose order changed (both sources and destinations, deduplicated). Use affectedParents to refresh your mental model of the tree without a follow-up get_children.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_paper-desktop_paper__write_html
tools.description:
IMPORTANT: Write incrementally. The user sees you write on the canvas in real-time. Show them visual progress every few seconds. Each write_html call should create one visual item: a header, a single list row, a button bar, or a paragraph block. Even simple components should be incremental: a card = container/header, then each row, then the footer. IMPORTANT: Prefer cloning instead of remaking existing Paper nodes using ``. For repeated elements: create the container first, then add each item as a separate write_html call into the container or use the duplicate tool on the first child. HTML and CSS rules: - Always use inline styles (style="..") - Enforce consistency with design tokens as CSS variables if available - All Google Fonts and locally installed fonts are available in font-family - All CSS color formats are supported: hex, rgb(a), hsl(a), oklch, oklab etc - Use flex as the primary layout mode. Flexbox, padding, and gap are the core layout tools in Paper's interface - Absolute position is fully supported. Use it for decorative elements. Avoid covering the entire artboard with a single absolute element, it blocks cursor interaction underneath - Do NOT use: margin, display: inline, display: grid, HTML tables. Use padding and gap for spacing - display: block is acceptable for simple elements (text, decorative shapes) but not for layout containers - Assume border-box sizing everywhere - Use 
 or white-space: pre for code blocks or indented text
- Do NOT use emojis as icons. Use SVG icons or images
- Rich text isn't supported in Paper; code snippets should be a single element with one text color and pre whitespace
- Use the layer-name attribute to set names on elements in the Paper layer tree, e.g. 

- Local images MUST use absolute paths in an img starting with paper-asset:// e.g. 
- paper-gen:// URLs generate AI images. ONLY if the user asked; read the "image-generation" guide first

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__delegate_task
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Delegate one task to a T3-owned child agent/subagent of THIS thread and run it with only the supplied task prompt, without copying parent conversation history. Choose providers and models from orchestrator_capabilities, which uses the same live catalog as the composer. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model. Use this for any model missing from the native tool, including same-provider work, for cross-provider work, or for explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For every T3 delegated review round, call delegate_task again with the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in the task prompt. Track each round by its own taskId and use a distinct clientRequestId per round, stable across retries of that round. The childThreadId is backing storage, not the target for starting another delegated review round through t3_thread_send. Set isolation to worktree for a separate checkout based on the parent local commit, with project setup completed before the child starts. Uncommitted edits are not copied; omitted isolation shares the parent checkout. Provider, model, model options (see orchestrator_capabilities), runtime mode, and interaction mode inherit unless target overrides them. A requested runtimeMode must be one the target provider lists in orchestrator_capabilities runtimeModes; an inherited one steps down to the broadest mode it offers. Leave runtimeMode unset unless the user asks for a supervised child: approval-required and auto-accept-edits usually make the child wait for a person at each action that needs approval. Prefer mode='async' for long work; mode='wait' blocks until completion, a blocking question, or timeout. If hasPendingQuestion, pass threadId=childThreadId to t3_pending_request_list, t3_pending_request_read (with requestId) and t3_pending_request_respond, or ask the user; the task's completion still wakes this thread. timeoutMs on mode=wait is only the parent's wait budget and does not cancel the child. waitTimedOut on that wait call means the timeout fired; keep that taskId and read status on later task_status. An async child's completion wakes this thread through a notification, steered into active turns where supported or queued otherwise, so end the turn instead of polling or spawning watchers; use task_status only when the result is needed mid-turn.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_preview
tools.description: Render an HTML page in T3's headless browser and get back a PNG screenshot, contentHeight (the height the page needs at this width), and its console output: log, info, warning, error, and uncaught exceptions, with stack traces pointing into page.html. console.log is a fine way to report your own checks. The page gets the theme variables and layout described in html_render.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_render
tools.description: Show a finished HTML page (chart, table, diagram, collage, mockup) inline in this thread, above your final text reply; call it before writing that reply. The reader already sees the page, so the reply should not announce it, say where it is, or restate it: add only what the page doesn't say. Preview with html_preview first. T3 fits the frame to the page's height at each reader's width. A height below the page's contentHeight caps the frame there, and the rest scrolls inside it. Write one self-contained document with inline <style> and <script>. Local images written as absolute file paths (src="/abs/shot.png", CSS url(/abs/bg.webp), or a JS string) are inlined automatically; remote http(s) URLs, such as a CDN chart library, load as-is. The frame is borderless on the thread's background, as wide as the reply column (728px on desktop by default, wider if the reader widens chat, about 360px on phones), and its left edge lines up with your reply text. The page sits on the thread's own background, so by default leave html, body, and the outermost element with no background color. This overrides general style preferences such as a fixed black page background. Use a fluid width with no horizontal padding on the outermost element, and no outer card, border, or banner title: the page is part of your reply. If a box needs its own background (a mock of a specific screen, a panel that must stand apart), give it at least 16px of padding on every side and var(--radius) corners, so content never touches its edge. Give charts fixed pixel heights rather than heights that scale with width. Let content set the page's height. Avoid viewport-based heights such as 100vh or height:100% on html or body; the frame grows to fit the page, so they can make it grow again and again. T3 injects its active theme as CSS custom properties on :root, and they follow the user's theme and light/dark mode live: --background (page background, identical to the thread around the frame), --foreground, --muted, --muted-foreground, --card, --card-foreground, --popover, --popover-foreground, --secondary, --secondary-foreground, --border, --input, --ring, --primary, --primary-foreground (solid buttons), --accent, --accent-foreground (brand accent), --accent-surface, --accent-surface-foreground, --destructive, --destructive-foreground, --destructive-surface, --warning, --warning-foreground, --warning-surface, --success, --success-foreground, --info, --info-foreground, --code-background, --code-foreground, --chart-1 ... --chart-6 (categorical series for charts), --radius, --font-sans, --font-mono. The base stylesheet sets html background/color/font from these, body margin to 0, and hides the page's scrollbar; your own CSS overrides it.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__schedule_task
tools.description: Create persistent work in the app scheduler that runs even when no turn is active. Pass schedule as a STRUCTURED OBJECT, never JSON text. Timers: {type:'interval', everyMs:3600000} is hourly; {type:'fixed_time', timeOfDay:'09:00', weekdays:[1,2,3,4,5]} is weekday mornings; report the returned nextRunAt. Webhooks: {type:'webhook'} runs once per request to a generated URL. The run sees the request ONLY through prompt placeholders: {{body.path}} (e.g. {{body.action}}, {{body.release.tag_name}}), {{headers.name}}, {{query.name}}, {{body}}, or {{request}} (method, headers with credentials redacted, and body). For a sender that signs requests, first call request_secret so the user enters the secret privately (never ask for it in chat or invent one), then set signature with the returned secretRef, e.g. GitHub: {type:'webhook', signature:{header:'x-hub-signature-256', encoding:'hex', prefix:'sha256=', secretRef}}. The result's webhookUrl is the public URL to give the user; if it is absent, this environment has no T3 Connect managed tunnel, so tell the user to enable T3 Connect remote access rather than sharing a path. Omit projectId for this thread's project. In this thread's project, runs post into THIS thread by default (bindToCurrentThread=true), which suits an orchestrator that sees every trigger, delegates work, and can dedupe against what is in flight; use false only when the user wants a fresh top-level thread per run. Elsewhere each run launches a fresh thread. Provider, model, and runtime settings inherit from this thread, or from the project default when there is no calling thread.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_launch
tools.description: Create an ordinary TOP-LEVEL thread with an explicit workspace binding before its agent starts. Use this when the user requests independent work, a new thread, or a PR stack in its own worktree; use delegate_task for child subagents. Set workspaceStrategy to {type:"worktree",baseRef:"parent-branch",branch:"new-branch",startFromOrigin:false} for a new worktree based on local commits, or {type:"existing_worktree",worktreePath:"/absolute/path",branch:"existing-branch"} to use an existing checkout. For upstream commits, set startFromOrigin:true. Omitted workspaceStrategy means the project root, NOT the caller's worktree. Omit projectId/modelSelection/modes to inherit those settings from the calling thread; a caller outside a T3 thread must pass projectId and gets the project's default model. Set scratch:true instead of projectId for a thread without a project: it runs in a fresh folder of its own, outside any repository. Put the task in message. Do not ask the agent to create its own worktree via shell: that does not update the thread binding. Each call creates a new launch with no retry key; retain threadId and use t3_thread_read/t3_thread_wait to follow preparation. To link a thread for the user, write `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with the threadId exactly as returned, not URL-encoded; T3 Code shows the thread's current title. After errors or lost responses, inspect t3_thread_list before retrying. Attachments must be pending uploads. The new thread may not run with broader runtime or interaction modes than the caller: the calling T3 thread's own modes, or the permission mode an outside agent was approved with.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_worktree_handoff
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Move this agent thread into a new git worktree. To launch a separate agent already bound to a new or existing worktree, use t3_thread_launch with workspaceStrategy instead. Creates the worktree branch (optionally from origin), re-points the thread at the worktree, and by default runs the project's setup script there. Changing the workspace detaches the live provider session, so the current turn ends shortly after the handoff is recorded; call this as the last action of the turn. To keep working after the handoff, pass continuationPrompt with the remaining work: it is queued as the thread's next message and starts a new turn inside the worktree with the conversation preserved. Without it the thread stays idle until the next message. The worktree is not removed automatically when the thread is deleted. Fails if the thread is already attached to a worktree.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__watch_pull_request
tools.description: Have T3 Code watch an open pull request for this thread, linking it first if needed. T3 Code checks it every two minutes and wakes you with a message when a check fails, the required checks pass, someone else comments or reviews, or the branch starts to conflict with its base. Use this to monitor or babysit a pull request instead of polling, sleeping, or running a watcher. Only comments posted after this call wake you, so handle the existing ones first, then end your turn. A wake is news, not a merge decision: check readiness yourself before merging. While T3 Code watches, the thread stays in the user's Working list, not their inbox. When you hand the work back to the user, call unwatch_pull_request first so the thread returns to their inbox. Watching ends when the pull request merges or closes, when its thread settles or is archived, when T3 Code fails to read it 8 times in a row (a host rate limit only delays it), when the user stops this thread, or when you call unwatch_pull_request. Unsettle the thread before starting a new watch. A subagent cannot watch: its parent thread owns the pull request.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__write_pull_request_guides
tools.description: Write review guides for up to 20 pull requests, the tour a maintainer reads in a pull request's Guide tab. content.content:
- How consistent are the typography, spacing, imagery and materials with the chosen direction? Judge these dimensions separately.
- Does this element violate a specific, recorded dislike?
- Does the primary action remain visually prominent in this captured state?
- Did this revision improve the intended quality while preserving the qualities already accepted?

Use element candidates and screenshot crops to ground findings. Clef can choose among known elements or assess a proposed observation; it does not automatically return a reliable free-form critique or locate every issue. The conversational model can draft observations, but explanations must remain tied to captured evidence and actual judgment results.

Keep cultural fit, coherence, novelty and usability visible as separate dimensions. Baste's existing weighted rubric remains configurable. Exact contrast, overflow, keyboard and functional checks stay deterministic. A visual model's confidence describes its answer distribution; Baste must measure agreement with user preferences before treating it as a reliable predictor. [TypeSafe confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence), [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring).

Evaluate pairwise choices on held-out screenshots and user decisions. Check order reversal, repeated judgments, mobile and desktop states, unusual styles and incomplete evidence. Generic decision benchmarks do not establish skill at aesthetic judgment. Preserve useful disagreements and diverse design candidates rather than optimizing everything toward one average appearance.

## Fluid interface

Keep the live design central. The partner has a compact, persistent animated presence with text entry, GPT-Live controls and optional captions. Its generated portrait is the loading and reduced-motion fallback. Discussion and tool results can attach to selected elements or expand inline. On narrow screens, use an anchored sheet with a clear return to the design. Preserve focus and in-progress edits when the interface changes.

Start with a small component catalog:

| Surface | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Partner choices | Compare the three initial characters |
| Evidence annotation | Point at a captured element and explain a reaction |
| Variant comparison | Compare current and proposed treatments |
| Palette and type controls | Adjust actual design values with a live preview |
| Reference board | Collect and relate visual references |
| Revision comparison | Inspect changes and undo them |
| Preference prompt | Resolve a meaningful taste question |

OpenUI composes these application-owned components and connects them to tools. Reactive state keeps ordinary controls responsive without a new model call for every click. Incremental changes preserve the controls and values that still apply. Actual design edits pass through the project's mutation tools, so a newly generated control never masquerades as a completed code change. [OpenUI architecture](https://www.openui.com/docs/openui-lang/architecture), [reactive state](https://www.openui.com/docs/openui-lang/reactive-state), [incremental editing](https://www.openui.com/docs/openui-lang/incremental-editing).

Keep Baste's Qwik/Panda stack and existing atelier identity. Evaluate a Qwik adapter around the framework-independent OpenUI core, including state subscriptions, query lifecycle, cancellation, action dispatch and component validation. Qwik support is adapter work, not a verified drop-in integration. Use one versioned component/tool contract rather than inventing a second generative UI grammar. Keep a normal static interface available if an emitted surface is invalid.

Popmelt's documented pattern is valuable here: element-level conversation, direct manipulation, local project context and a remembered history of design choices. Explore an optional in-page companion for connected projects, backed by the same Baste commands, so work can happen both in Studio and on the running site. This plan uses those interaction ideas; it does not claim Popmelt itself is integrated or that its advertised behavior was tested. [Popmelt](https://popmelt.com/).

## Tool and project contract

Introduce durable, account-scoped `Project`, `DesignPartner`, `Conversation`, `Evidence`, `DecisionEvent` and `Revision` records, with versioned character media manifests and live-session operation records. A project references its brief, selected audience persona, partner, connected sites, canonical design state, artifacts and active runs. Large evidence, media and conversation records are stored separately and referenced by ID.

All surfaces call the same validated service commands: agent, Studio, generated UI, CLI and MCP. Proposed tool families are partner creation/selection, profile inspection/refinement/pinning/revert, character media generation and bounded expression selection, live-session lifecycle, browser observation/navigation, reference collection, visual judgment, token/component edits, project patches, comparison/revert and speech. Tool schemas describe actual capabilities; the model cannot invent tools or obtain authority from page content.

Mutations include a base revision and idempotency key, and return the resulting revision, changed entities and a human-readable result. Apply changes atomically where possible. For connected repositories, stage a bounded patch, verify it, apply it and capture the updated preview; retain enough history to undo the patch without overwriting later user edits. A failed or interrupted action retains an accurate status. Newer edits take precedence over stale tool results.

The user's selected collaboration scope covers the connected project. The runtime still distinguishes project edits from external publication, payment and unrelated sites. Implement the browser as an isolated service with project-specific sessions, destination checks on navigation and subresources, and explicit capture/action history. Existing static decomposition is not this browser runtime.

Not Organic remains the hosted identity, wallet and provider boundary. GPT-Live already has a gateway endpoint and accounting: consume them through Baste's relay and add the existing `realtime:connect` capability to Baste's account flow. Inventory the provider's other existing routes before adding Baste adapters for chat, visual judgment, character media and speech; extend provider contracts only for demonstrated gaps. Credentials remain server-held. Budget a run across conversation, live-session duration, captures, judgments, media and speech, and stop further dispatch when cancelled or out of budget. Baste's current image/Jev client does not yet connect these additional workflows.

## Learning from decisions

Record candidate exposure and order, selection, interview answers, preference answers, automatic persona refinements, accepted edits, reversions and explicit reasons as typed events. Include relevant trait snapshots, evidence/revision IDs and model/rubric versions so a decision can be understood later. Automatic project personalization consumes these events during normal work; product analytics remains a separate projection.

Project history retains the detailed work context. The product analytics projection contains decision events and traits, following the recovered choice; raw conversation, voice recordings, screenshots and provider credentials are excluded from that projection. A candidate selection is not a negative label for every trait of the alternatives. Distinguish explicit preference, inferred preference, no response and technical failure.

Use these events first to improve ranking and measure usefulness: whether judgments match later choices, whether changes survive, and where users reverse the partner. Fine-tuning is a later experiment once there is enough representative, appropriately scoped evidence. Do not silently turn every logged event into a training example.

## Existing foundations and gaps

The source review found reusable foundations, but no complete conversational partner workflow:

- `src/persona/types.ts`, `builder.ts` and `store.ts`: cultural persona records; add partner identity and project context around them.
- `src/assets/generators.ts`: hosted image generation suitable for portrait jobs; add portrait-specific output and identity handling.
- `src/evaluation/typesafe-judge.ts`: explicit text-only Jev evidence; add a multimodal decision adapter and reusable rubrics without claiming existing pixel inspection.
- `src/notorganic/scope.ts` and account stores: reuse DID ownership for all new records and assets.
- `.flue/agents/baste.ts`: currently action dispatch with an unused session, not a persisted conversational tool loop.
- `src/decompose/index.ts`: static extraction and a short-lived optional browser path; add persistent observation/action sessions and browser network enforcement.
- `src/versioning/`: semantic changes and diffs; extend this into complete project revisions. The current OpenPencil import does not preserve the complete edited design as a reversible project mutation.
- `src/mcp/server.ts` and `src/gui/api.ts`: extract shared commands before allowing hosted partners to use them; current local MCP handlers are not account-scoped.
- `site/src/components/studio/`: preserve the existing components, but introduce a project work surface and shared generated contracts instead of extending duplicated API types indefinitely.

Twyne references to reuse as patterns are `src/components/onboarding/conversational-interview.tsx` for progressive briefing, `src/utils/personas.ts` for character voice and critical method, `src/components/in-flow/catalog.ts` and `src/utils/in-flow-tools.ts` for bounded tool surfaces, and its flow/review and brief-history utilities for visible state and durable decisions. Twyne's existing cast does not already implement generated partner identities. These are current source references, including work in progress, rather than proof of deployed behavior.

For GPT-Live, Twyne's `src/utils/live-voice.ts`, `src/utils/live-voice-workspace.ts`, `src/components/ui/live-voice-desk.tsx` and `convex/liveVoice.ts` provide local references for persona context, client delegation, revision-aware actions and Not Organic session authorization. Verify interruption against actual playback when adapting them; the inspected helper does not expose a separate output-queue clear operation. Keating's `web/src/components/KeatingBot.tsx` and `keating-bot.css` provide a discrete-pose atlas player with loading fallback, visibility pausing and reduced motion. Reuse those playback patterns in Qwik; generate new partner-specific art. Keating's separate Realtime interruption protocol must not be copied into GPT-Live as if they were the same API. These references were inspected in source, without a live provider or playback test.

The concrete Baste Live integration gaps are in `src/notorganic/server.ts` (request `realtime:connect`, bridge existing GET/POST `/v1/realtime/consent`, and represent Live availability), `src/gui/server.ts` (authenticated same-origin WebSocket upgrade/relay), `site/vite.config.ts` (WebSocket forwarding), and the new browser audio/delegation adapter. Existing grants may need reconnection for the additional scope. Reuse origin/CSRF protection for consent changes and check origin, account ownership and spending ceilings on the socket upgrade. Session budgeting must consume Not Organic's existing Live reservation contract; image/Jev request estimates do not cover an ongoing voice session.

## Build sequence and acceptance

| Stage | Deliverable | Acceptance evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Shared foundation | Project/partner schemas, ownership, commands, revisions, event contract and mappings to existing hosted capabilities | Account isolation; reload persistence; stale-write rejection; exact edit/undo round trip |
| 2. Meet and talk | Three persisted candidates, generated portraits, selection, core stop-motion assets, streamed conversation and automatic persona refinement | Interview the chosen partner; observe a supported profile revision and changed subsequent recommendation; reload and retain the same identity and learned context; undo or pin a trait; generated motions retain identity and individual failures recover |
| 3. Look together | Connected browser, captures, element references, Clef adapter and Jev decisions | Navigate a real site, capture desktop/mobile states, receive grounded judgments and reject stale evidence |
| 4. Collaborate | Initial OpenUI catalog, live controls, token/component tools and connected source patches | Discuss an element, adjust it through a generated surface, see the actual preview update, undo and reload without loss |
| 5. Live character | GPT-Live with shared tool delegation, generated stop-motion performance, individual spoken replies, project decision history and analytics projection | Real microphone/speaker session; speak over a reply; complete and cancel tool work with accurate state; refine the persona by voice; motion follows audible playback; reconnect without duplicate edits; close and reconcile usage; reduced-motion fallback; analytics contains only its allowed event fields |

After Stage 1, character/conversation and motion assets, browser/visual judgment, the Qwik OpenUI adapter, and Baste's relay/client for the existing Not Organic GPT-Live endpoint can proceed in parallel against shared contracts. Stage 4 integrates design tools; Stage 5 connects the live performance to that workflow. The first complete release includes GPT-Live and generated stop-motion characters. Broader project integrations follow later.

The first acceptance journey is deliberately end to end: describe a project, meet three characters, choose one, see its generated stop-motion presence, start GPT-Live, interview it and observe automatic refinement, open a connected site, discuss a specific element aloud, interrupt and clarify, compare an alternative informed by the refined persona, make and undo a real edit through the shared tools, end the call, then reload and continue with the learned profile intact. Verify actual audible output, animation and completed mutations separately. Passing that journey is the release goal, rather than merely completing the individual adapters.

content.thinking:
This is a large feature, and Stage 4 of the plan depends on a Project/partner foundation that only partially exists, so I need to scope out a realistic, honest implementation. I'm thinking through how the library definitions need to be shared between the server-side prompt generation and the client renderer, given that the site runs on Qwik while the root is the API server, and weighing options for how to structure that shared catalog.

I'm considering whether to put the catalog in the site's lib directory and generate a committed component-spec.json for the server to consume, or instead place the catalog in the root source and have the site import it directly—checking whether the site already imports from root for things like api-types. Since lang-core's library creation is generic over the component type, the catalog itself can stay framework-independent while each side supplies its own rendering.

Now I'm thinking through the Qwik adapter: the runtime (store, query manager, streaming parser, evaluation) needs to be wrapped with noSerialize since it's client-only, while the evaluated element tree stays plain JSON and serializable so it can live in a signal. Components would receive the node as props plus a context providing signals and QRL callbacks for setState/triggerAction, since QRLs serialize fine even though the runtime object itself doesn't.

For the server side, I'm considering how the model should generate OpenUI Lang alongside normal conversation bubbles — either as a dedicated surface endpoint or a combined response where the model streams text followed by an OpenUI block, leveraging the existing streaming parser in lang-core.

Now I'm figuring out what tools the design partner actually needs: token queries, a preview mechanism, and an apply_tokens mutation that writes into the persona's brand kit through the existing saveBrandKit flow, tracked with a base revision and idempotency key so edits route through the project's real mutation system rather than faking a completed change. I should check how the DesignVersionRegistry fits in and confirm the hosted site stays account-only.

Brand kit writes in hosted mode seem account-scoped, so I need to check how loadBrandKit resolves that scope and whether saving a brand kit for a base persona like cyberbotanist is even permitted given they can't be overwritten. Then there's the bigger architectural question of where this generated design-editing surface should actually live — inside Studio where a persona and tokens tab already exist, or in the public-facing conversation component used on the homepage and fitting room, since mutating design probably belongs in Studio's project context rather than the public surfaces.

Given the scale of the plan, the most natural integration point seems to be the conversation's existing hand-rolled attachment system, since replies already attach rendered content — I could replace those hand-rolled attachment kinds with an OpenUI catalog, letting AI-mode replies generate live OpenUI surfaces and demo-mode replies use pre-authored OpenUI Lang programs instead.

I'm also weighing whether conversations require an account in AI mode, since mutating tokens from the anonymous homepage feels off — maybe the right design is a client-local reactive preview state for the live garment specimen, with a separate "apply" mutation that persists into the user's brand kit within Studio.

Rather than overcomplicate this with too many integration options, I'll make a reasonable call: use the existing partner conversation surface plus the Studio brand-kit/project for mutations, but first I want to check converseAvailable's account requirements, the brand kit's account scope, and whether Studio already has a tailor/fitting panel with live preview before settling on this.

For font overrides, I want a shared pure function that builds the font stack consistently -- the server already has `applyDesign(tokens, overrides)` in src/projects/design.ts, and I need the client to reuse that same logic rather than reimplementing it.

Having the server return the font stacks directly in the options payload makes client-side application trivial -- it just assigns colors, looks up font stacks, and looks up radii. Now I'm sketching the final catalog of Qwik renderer components: a root Surface, a Group for layout (stack/row/grid), a Note for tone-based text, and a ColorField bound to a color role enum.

I'm defining FontField for heading/body font selection, a general ChoiceField for arbitrary option sets (preferred over a specific EdgeField), a DesignPreview component for live rendering of colors/fonts/edges, and a Variants/Variant pair for compact side-by-side comparisons.

Rounding this out, I want a ContrastCheck component for deterministic WCAG ratio/level reporting, Swatches for color display, a Question/Button/Buttons set for preference prompts with emphasis levels, and I'll fold Status into Note using a tone attribute rather than creating a separate component. For functions, I'm planning an @Contrast(fg, bg) helper that returns a rounded ratio.

Now for tools, I'm sketching a read_design() that returns revision, color roles, fonts, edges, and overrides read-only, paired with update_design() and restore_design() mutations. I'm thinking I should fold design_history into read_design as a trailing list of recent revisions rather than a separate call, and I need to account for edge/font enums being generated server-side from token definitions.

Font fields can stay typed as plain strings, with validity described via the enum in the tool schema rather than enforced client-side, since the server validates mutations anyway. For file layout, I'm placing catalog schemas in one module (name-only, no component references), letting a separate registry map names to actual Qwik components, and having a build script emit the compiled catalog JSON that becomes the prompt spec.

I should add a drift guard — a site test confirming the committed JSON matches a freshly computed spec. Dependency-wise, I need `@openuidev/lang-core` and `zod@^4` added to the site's dependencies (not devDependencies, since these are runtime), plus lang-core added at the root too, and I need to make sure the catalog imports zod from the same `"zod/v4"` path lang-core uses so introspection works against a single shared instance.

I also want to check whether lang-core has any postinstall scripts or other telemetry beyond the opt-in runtime flag, verifying this during install. For bundling, since lang-core plus zod is sizable, I should keep the import inside a dynamic `import()` within the Qwik `useVisibleTask$` so it only loads lazily in the Studio workbench rather than polluting other bundles.

Since Studio's /gui route is client-heavy, SSR will render the workbench shell with a "Preparing the surface…" placeholder until the visible task kicks in. I'm also confirming that recursive component$ definitions work fine in Qwik since rendering is lazy, so a Node component rendering itself for children is safe, and each catalog renderer will receive plain JSON props plus context access for setting bindings, running plans, and streaming options.

Context values need to stay serializable, so I'm using QRLs and a store marked with noSerialize where needed. For reactive bindings, I walk the evaluated props tree replacing ReactiveAssign placeholders with resolved values from the store, so components subscribe to store changes and the whole tree re-evaluates and re-renders on each update — which is fine at this scale, even for rapid-fire events like color input dragging.

Since Qwik compares props by identity, new objects trigger full re-renders of all nodes, but keyed diffing by child index should preserve DOM elements and avoid focus/caret issues as long as I set values idempotently. I'm now porting the action-triggering runtime logic (equivalent to Vue's implementation) to handle plan step execution.

For the workbench side, I need to route OpenUrl requests through a safe-open check, forward mutations via fireMutation, and support custom action events without explicit steps. On the error-handling front, the runtime should collect parse/runtime/query/mutation errors and surface them in a quiet disclosure UI, while also giving independent honest feedback -- like a toast confirming a design was saved as a new version -- separate from whatever the model's own UI shows. I'm now thinking through what should happen in the Projects flow once the update_design tool call returns.

When update_design completes and returns a new revision, I need the callback to update project detail without wiping unsaved brief/audience drafts the way a full "all" reset would. I'm leaning toward a new "design" field mode that rebases baseRevision to the new value (avoiding a stale conflict warning) while preserving the existing name/brief/audience drafts, since a design-only change doesn't touch those fields and rebasing is safe as long as the draft wasn't already stale.

I also need to check that update_details validates baseRevision against current revision so a brief save following a design save correctly uses the rebased draft, confirm restore_revision restores design along with everything else in the project history, and plan persistence of conversation threads per project in localStorage with program/turns/state, including a reset mechanism. For the model call itself, I'm following the existing streaming pattern — direct fetch with SSE parsing, timeout-based abort tied to client disconnect, capped tokens around 1800, temperature 0.4 — and now need to work out the message format sent to the model, starting with a system preamble.

The final user message includes the current program, unsaved control values, saved design state, and the request text, plus optional hidden context. On the server I validate the model's response by extracting a code fence as a patch, merging it into the existing program, parsing to confirm it's valid with no errors, and falling back to a single repair attempt before rejecting; I also need to cap program size at 24KB and ensure security by restricting generated surfaces to only the three permitted tool calls plus OpenUrl.

Then I'm mapping out the NDJSON streaming protocol: delta events carry raw text, a final done event bundles the prose, merged program (or null if unchanged), acceptance flag, and optional notice, and error events report failures mid-stream since HTTP status can't be changed once streaming begins — pre-stream validation failures still go through the normal JSON error response.

For testing, I'm planning root tests covering project command updates and the fence-extraction/validation/merge logic against catalog.json, plus site-level tests for the OpenUI runtime — parsing the starter program, binding updates, actions, mutation tooling, event dispatch, and catalog drift checks — followed by manual browser QA running the dev servers and opening Studio.

This is a large build, so I should check the memory notes on dev servers and Playwright setup before diving into the projects tests.

I'm building Stage 4: a Qwik adapter porting OpenUI's state/query/mutation logic, a zod-defined Baste control catalog with live preview, real design read/update/restore tools backed by revisioned commands, and a partner endpoint that streams and validates patches with a fallback surface. Next I'll check my notes on dev servers and existing test patterns.

- T3 restarts kill background shells (dev servers included). Start them detached: `setsid nohup node scripts/runtime.mjs site > /tmp/baste-site.log 2>&1 &`, with `api` for the API on :3456. Add `--voice-from-skate` to the API to load the fal key.

- Open the Studio at `http://localhost:5173`, not `127.0.0.1`: the API rejects that Host (403 "Invalid host"), so the Studio silently falls back to demo mode.
- Playwright lives in `~/.cache/baste-shots/node_modules` (not in the repo). QA scripts go in that directory. Run them with `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH` and `executablePath: '/usr/bin/google-chrome'`. Add `--enable-unsafe-webgpu --enable-features=Vulkan --use-angle=vulkan` for the shader pages (/method, fitting room).
- Playwright's recordVideo is CSS-pixel sized (1440×900 for a 1440×900 viewport).
- In dev, the "Click-to-Source: Alt" overlay shows in the first ~3.5 s of every page, so recorded takes are cut after 3.6 s.

Since the test harness's mocked `res` lacks `on`/`write`, I'll test streamSurface directly and cover the handler's 503 path separately. On the client side, I'm adding read_design and update_design functions to the projects library, wiring them to the GET design endpoint and the POST command endpoint using the current project's baseRevision.

I need to decide where ProjectDesign lives — probably duplicate a lightweight client-side type in lib/projects.ts rather than sharing it with the server's design.ts shape, since site types already mirror server ones elsewhere. For the surface client, I'm writing NDJSON stream parsing plus a small client-side version of the server's splitReply logic, accepting some duplication since it's a small function and both sides get tested independently.

Now I'm shifting to the Qwik components, following the existing pattern of using useVisibleTask$ with noSerialize controllers, and sketching out the OpenUISurface component signature with program, streaming, and tools props.

Since tools are functions and can't cross the component$ boundary as plain props, I'm designing the Surface to own its own SurfaceRuntime created inside useVisibleTask$, built from props like apiBase, projectId, an onSaved$ QRL, and a revision getter, with tool implementations closing over the relevant signals. I'm sketching a single DesignWorkbench component that takes projectId, revision, apiBase, csrfToken, onSaved$, and surfaceAvailable as props, loads the design on revision changes, and maintains program text, turns, pending/streaming state, and errors in a store persisted to localStorage per project. The runtime wraps a SurfaceRuntime whose tools read the design via fetch and update it through runProjectCommand with the current revision, invoking onSaved$ afterward, while a snapshot signal gets updated via onChange by cloning the runtime's current tree and errors into a view signal.

For rendering, I'm planning a recursive SurfaceNode component fed by view.value.root, with a SurfaceCtx context providing QRL-based assign$ and run$ actions plus design metadata and a busy flag -- noting that QRLs are serializable so this works fine in Qwik even though the runtime itself is non-serializable. I'm weighing component$ recursion versus inline function components for SurfaceNode, since inline components are simpler but can't use hooks like useContext, which matters since SurfaceNode needs access to the context.

I'll use component$ for each catalog component that needs useContext, mapping node.typeName to component with props drawn from evaluated ElementNode.props and children that may be nodes, strings, or null. For the preview rendering, I'm checking how Garment resolves persona fittings for custom personas versus base ones, since fittings and fittingIcons are keyed by persona.id and I need to confirm the fallback behavior.

I still need fittingVars from full DesignTokens for the server tokens, and I'm sketching the Variant component as a small specimen preview with a heading, body text, primary button, and a "Try this" action trigger. For contrast checking I'll either find an existing WCAG utility in the site lib or write one quickly, and SaveStatus just needs to render idle/loading/success/error states based on the mutation result shape.

For the action buttons I'm distinguishing "cut" (commit/save, primary emphasis) from "baste" or "pin" (reversible try, secondary), disabling them while streaming. Then I'm laying out the remaining field types: Choice as a bound radio group, FontField as a select with a live font preview line, EdgeField as a five-way segmented control with corner glyphs, ColorField combining a color picker with a hex text input that commits on valid input, and Section/Workbench as grouping containers for titles and children.

For layout I'm thinking of making the Workbench a CSS grid where Preview, Compare, Question, and Note span the full width while Sections fill individual cells, with the whole thing placed as a new "Design workbench" panel in the Projects flow between the audience panel and history, stacking on narrow screens and using a chat column plus surface area on wider ones.

For error handling, I'm planning a fallback message if the root surface is missing during runtime errors, and a smaller disclosure noting omitted parts if errors occur but the root still renders. I'm also working out persistence using a versioned localStorage key scoped by project to store the program, turns, and state.

I need to track whether a program originates as a starter or partner build, since starter programs should regenerate their defaults when the underlying design changes after a save — while preserving any state values the user has already customized, since those take precedence over regenerated defaults.

For undo semantics: resetting unsaved changes should restore the declared defaults, which after a starter regen become the new saved values. For undoing a save itself, I'm considering whether the project history panel should let users restore a whole version snapshot, or offer a more granular "undo this design change" option that calls restore_design targeting the prior revision specifically for design_updated entries.

Since restoring to revision-1 is only an exact undo if that's the latest design change (otherwise it also reverts later changes), I think the clearest approach is a simple "Last saved: version N · Undo" control in the workbench that reverts to the design state just before the most recent save.

I also need to make sure the history list copy mentions restoring brief, audience, and design together, and crucially the save flow from the workbench must not clobber unsaved draft fields—so I want a new "design" mode for acceptDetail that only updates the design while preserving the user's current name/brief/audience drafts.

Then for baseRevision: since design-only saves don't touch the brief fields, it's safe to update the draft's baseRevision to the new project revision while keeping the stale brief/audience content, so the "newer version" warning won't fire incorrectly after a design save.

On the workbench side, I'll have it pull revision from the project's current detail so it stays in sync as brief saves happen, and have the component read csrfToken/apiBase directly from StudioCtx rather than threading them as props, passing project, revisions, and an onSaved$ QRL that calls acceptDetail with "design" mode.

content.thinking:
Now I'm planning the workbench component's responsibilities: loading the design per project, managing starter/partner program state persisted locally, handling runtime creation reactively, rendering the surface through context, supporting partner conversation with streaming replies, and enabling undo of the last design.

I'm structuring the Qwik state object with design loading status, program/draft/turns tracking for the partner flow, runtime view snapshots, and persisted saved state, alongside a non-serialized signal holding the actual runtime instance.

I'm sketching the three visible tasks: one to fetch the design and restore persisted state, one to instantiate the runtime and sync snapshots back into state with cleanup on dispose, and one to push the current or draft program into the runtime whenever it changes.

For the tool implementations, I'm defining read_design to pull the stored reading and update_design to validate changes, run the update command against the server with revision tracking, and surface the result. I'm now reasoning through an edge case where a model-generated mutation sends unchanged values equal to what's already saved, which the server correctly rejects with a 400 "already saved" error -- tracing through how normalizeDesign strips values matching the generated base so the starter mutation's full-value payload still resolves safely against the saved revision.

For revision freshness inside the closure, I'm relying on the store proxy to give me the current value at call time rather than a captured value, and command IDs are regenerated per mutation with query manager loading state preventing duplicate fires. After a successful save, the flow accepts the detail and revision changes propagate to trigger reloads and invalidate dependent queries elsewhere in the program. For persistence, I'm sketching out a versioned storage key scoped by project that saves origin, program, turns, and state, debounced on changes, while considering whether account/DID scoping needs to be baked into that key too.

I'm defining the partner send function: a guarded async generator that sets pending/error state, pushes the prior program and turn, opens an abortable stream, accumulates delta text into a draft program, and on completion pushes the partner's reply and swaps in the new program while resetting pending/draft state afterward, with cleanup in a finally block. I'm also noting edge cases — draftProgram handling a full first-turn program, and the need to guard against stale responses if the project changes mid-stream.

If a project switch unmounts the Workbench, I should key it by project id and abort the stream in cleanup. For partner unavailability, I'm considering fetching health status upfront to disable the composer with an explanation rather than letting a send attempt fail with a 503. I'm also sketching a "start over from saved design" control that resets origin, program, and turns by bumping a reset key the runtime task watches, and starting to think through how to implement undo for the last save based on revision history.

For undoing a save, I need to inspect the latest revision entry — if it's a design update or restore, the undo button should call restore_design targeting the prior revision, passing the latest revision as a prop. I'm also designing error display for the surface view: showing a fallback message with a return button if the root is missing, or a collapsible list of dropped-part errors otherwise, including tool runtime errors like network failures. Then I'm setting up the rendering with a context provider wrapping the surface node, sharing assign/run handlers, lock state, design, and persona through a shared store.

Since the design can be null before loading finishes, I realize the context needs to be provided unconditionally, so I'm splitting the component: an outer Workbench handles loading state, while an inner SurfaceHost receives the loaded design and persona and provides the context, with the runtime handlers passed down as props. For handling action events, I'm mapping continue_conversation to sending a message with context, and deciding how to handle open_url actions — leaning toward ignoring them with a notice that generated links aren't opened, though I'm weighing whether to allow safe https links to open in a new tab instead.

I'm settling on ignoring open_url actions entirely since untrusted model output linking to arbitrary sites is a phishing risk, and confirming that onAction can be passed as a plain callback option to the runtime that invokes the send QRL. For persona preview, I'll pass the project's audience snapshot as a prop, and now I'm ready to write the workbench component itself, accounting for the flow's design acceptDetail mode, history hints, and panel placement.

The overlapping sticky top bar in the screenshot is just the fixed header showing through in the element capture, so that's not a real bug.

Looking at smaller details like the pressed state indicator on "Geometric" and the dashed styling on "Undo unsaved changes" — these seem intentional and fine. Let me actually debug the Contrast function directly in node to figure out why it's not resolving as expected.

Preview, color binding, and save all work correctly—preview turned teal and saved as version 2. Two bugs remain though: contrast is stuck reading "waiting for two colours" and undo stalled, so I'll tackle contrast first.

content.thinking:
I realize the bug: the `hex` schema object is shared across fields, so marking it reactive for one field mutates the shared object and makes every field using it reactive too. The fix is to ensure `bound()` operates on a fresh clone of the schema rather than the shared instance.

This likely affects font fields too, since optional wrappers might get unwrapped when checking reactivity. I also need to regenerate the catalog and add a test confirming that Contrast's prompt signature stays free of `$binding`.

`bound(hex)` was marking the shared hex schema object itself as reactive, turning every prop (including Contrast) into a `$binding` and leaking into prompt signatures. I'll fix this by marking a clone instead.

No Qwik errors showing up. I'm tracing through how Qwik's rendering actually works under the hood—how a component tree gets processed, props get updated on children, and rendering gets scheduled and patched once promises resolve.

If any child's render promise never resolves, the whole commit hangs, so I'm checking which component could be stuck: DesignWorkbench's useVisibleTask$, SurfaceHost's useTask$ tracking props.design, Garment's locale/style hooks. Comparing the save path (which worked, DOM updated) against the undo path (which didn't)—the key difference seems to be that undo is triggered from a handler inside DesignWorkbench where the button's own label and disabled state depend on props that change during the same re-render, which might be causing the hang.

Since the QRL itself completes fully (logs confirm 'undo accepted' then the finally block runs) but no commit happens even seconds later, I suspect the issue lies in how Qwik handles invocation context when a child's QRL calls a parent's QRL (like onSaved$) that mutates the parent's store while the child's handler is still considered in-flight—this cross-context invocation might be what's breaking the render commit.

A common workaround would be to avoid awaiting the parent QRL directly and instead defer it with a setTimeout, which would confirm whether this is indeed an invocation-context issue. I'm also reconsidering the first run's behavior: the undo click produced no POST at all, suggesting that maybe the click handler's QRL itself was referencing stale state after the save's re-render, even though the undo button visually appeared.

No errors are showing, so the render commit is hanging silently—likely because calling the parent's `onSaved$` QRL from within the child's in-flight click QRL confuses Qwik's invocation context. I'll test this by deferring the call.

content.thinking:
I'm confirming that on the committed HEAD code, saving the brief still shows "Saved" status even though the server version is ahead — which means the local draft's name must actually already match the updated name, so the chip's "Saved" label is technically correct but misleading about the version number being stale.

I suspect this is a Qwik fine-grained binding issue: the revision text is bound via a derived signal tied to the original project object captured at render, and when that object gets replaced wholesale on the detail event, Qwik's signal binding doesn't get rebound to the new object's revision property, leaving the displayed number frozen at its old value even as the rest of the component re-renders.

The "Unsaved changes" detection worked because the draft store mutations happen in place, unlike the detail object replacement.

I'm thinking the real fix is to avoid relying on replaced objects for props bindings, since replacing `f.detail` wholesale likely breaks Qwik's signal rebinding during re-render — this smells like a known Qwik vdom diffing issue where signal-bound text nodes don't rebind to a new signal on full re-render.

Possible workarounds: force element recreation by keying on revision, try a template literal to sidestep the _fnSignal optimization, or just fix the root cause by mutating `f.detail` in place instead of replacing it wholesale.

But this general fix has a gap -- deleted properties like a removed design field won't get cleaned up by Object.assign, so I'd need to explicitly delete stale keys too. I'm second-guessing whether this theory even matches the symptom though, since "Saved" updates correctly while the revision chip doesn't, so I want to trace through the conditional expression logic depending on drafts before committing to this fix.

Actually, this confirms the theory: `changed` is computed as a plain boolean constant in the component body, so it reflects fresh values, while the revision chip is bound directly in JSX to a stale object reference. So the fix is to update `f.detail` in place rather than replacing it, which I'll implement as a small helper that merges a new object's properties onto the existing one.

For nested fields like `design` or `audience`, a shallow merge isn't enough since replacing those nested objects would leave any JSX bound directly to their sub-properties stuck on stale references. I need a recursive deep-sync for plain objects and arrays, though arrays rendered through `.map()` in the render body should already re-render correctly since that's recomputed fresh each time.

I'm also weighing a workaround where I force a remount of the whole detail subtree keyed on revision changes, but that risks losing focus and transient state, which feels too jarring just to work around this binding issue.

The cleaner fix is computing a local const like `revision = p.revision` in the render body so it's captured per-render rather than fnSignal-bound, then using that local wherever JSX reads the prop directly, including fixing the adjacent chip bug the same way. But I realize this pattern is widespread across ProjectsFlow's JSX — things like `p.name`, `p.audience?.name`, and the audience summary panel could all show stale data after a save, so I need to check how far this spreads before deciding on a targeted versus broader fix.

I confirmed this is a pre-existing Studio bug (the revision chip lags the server's version) that my feature just exposed, likely because Qwik's optimizer binds the JSX signal to the old project object while `acceptDetail` replaces rather than mutates it. I'll check the compiled module to verify this theory.

## The Studio

```bash
npx baste gui        # local API on :3456 — then open the site's /gui route
```

The Studio (`site/`, route `/gui`) puts one persona at the centre: see it **wearing its own design** (a live
try-on of the same screen in its tokens, with contrast checks), export tokens, draft prompts and generate assets
with a staged progress view, pin a moodboard, read a decomposed brand kit, teach it your taste, and edit tokens
as an OpenPencil document. Without a local server it runs in demo mode on the built-in personas.

Start the API and Qwik Studio together from the repository root:

```bash
devenv tasks run baste:install
devenv up
```

Open `http://localhost:5173/gui/` for the Studio and `http://localhost:5173/docs/` for documentation.
The site proxies `/api` to the Baste API on port 3456. Storybook is opt-in.
See [local development](docs/development.md) for tasks, port overrides and verification boundaries.

content.text:
OpenUI is now implemented in Baste. It's a **workbench** on each Studio project that has an audience: an interactive surface for the project's colours, typefaces and corner style, where a design partner (AI) can rebuild the surface when you ask it to.

**How it works**
- **The surface.** Baste uses OpenUI's core package (`@openuidev/lang-core`) with a Qwik adapter I wrote (`site/src/lib/openui/runtime.ts` and `site/src/components/openui/`). OpenUI doesn't ship one for Qwik. Changing a colour, typeface or corner style updates the live preview straight away, with no model call. Contrast is measured, never written in by the model.
- **Saving.** Nothing is saved until you press a save button. Each save becomes a numbered project version, so you can undo it from the workbench or restore it from the project history. Two new project commands back this: `update_design` and `restore_design`.
- **The partner.** You ask for a change and the reply streams in as an edit to the surface; values you've already changed are kept. The server checks every edit against the list of allowed components and actions. If an edit is invalid it gets one repair attempt; if that also fails, your current surface stays. The partner can't save anything itself, open links or call a write action outside a button you press.
- **Without a model,** Baste shows its own built-in surface and the controls still work. The partner needs a local server with `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Hosted accounts don't use the server's key, so they only get Baste's surface.
- **One shared definition.** The browser and the server both read the component and action list in `site/src/lib/openui/catalog.ts`. After editing it, run `npm run openui:catalog` in `site/`; tests fail until you do.
- **Saved locally.** The partner conversation and its surface are kept in the browser's localStorage per account and project, not on the server. Design changes themselves are saved as project versions.

**Verification**
- Tests: all 215 root tests and 25 site tests pass, as do typecheck, lint and the production build.
- In the browser I created a project, then edited, saved and undid a change, and the colour came back exactly. The live partner built a working comparison of two heading typefaces, and "Try Monoton" switched the preview's headline. The surface survived a reload, and the page doesn't scroll sideways at 390 px.

**Things you should know**
- **Qwik stale-display bug.** After a save, the project panel kept showing the old version. On the committed code this also showed up after "Save brief", though it only stuck permanently once the workbench was added. The cause: Qwik kept reading the project object from before the save. I fixed it in `projects.tsx` by rendering from a fresh copy of the project and passing the workbench its values directly.
- **Partner quality.** The partner usually produces valid surfaces, but in one run its comparison cards didn't change the preview. I tightened the instructions it gets; that wording isn't covered by an automated test.
- **Revoked key.** The `openai-api` key in Skate is revoked, but `openai_api_key` works. I updated my notes accordingly.
- **Telemetry.** `@openuidev/lang-core` runs an install script that sends a usage event unless `OPENUI_TELEMETRY_DISABLED` is set. npm held the script back here, and the Dockerfile now sets that variable. Telemetry at runtime is off by default.
- **Not done yet** from the plan's list: choosing between three partners, element annotation, the reference board, revision comparison, and patches to connected source code. The plan has a note recording what's done.

Nothing is committed. The working tree also has your unrelated in-progress changes (vector scripts, `generators.ts`, `quiver.ts`, `fal.test.ts`), so I left committing to you.
